common_name: Korean Gold Plum Yew (Golden Japanese Plum Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil where a few hours of morning sun will reach the plant; too much shade fades the gold color to plain green, while hot afternoon sun can scorch the needles.

directions: This narrow, pillar-shaped selection of Japanese plum yew pushes lemon-yellow new growth each spring that gradually mellows to green by summer, giving the plant a two-toned, glowing appearance during its active flush. It is slow-growing and columnar rather than spreading, making it useful as a vertical accent or narrow screen where space is tight beneath high tree canopy. A half-day of gentle morning light intensifies the gold color without the leaf burn that full sun exposure causes in hot climates; deep shade keeps the plant safe but mutes the coloring to ordinary green. Like other plum yews it shrugs off deer browsing, heavy soil, and root competition, needing only patience given its slow annual growth rate.

common_name: Gnome Plum Yew (Dwarf Mounding Japanese Plum Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial to full shade; this Hillier-raised selection stays low and rounded, so give it space to widen rather than expecting upward growth.

directions: Originating as a Hillier Nurseries selection, this dwarf plum yew forms a tight, rounded mound that stays well under two feet tall while gradually broadening outward, with shorter and noticeably stiffer needles than the species that give the foliage a denser, bristlier texture. It works well as a durable low mass planting or foundation shrub in permanently shaded beds where taller conifers would eventually overwhelm the space. Growth is slow and even, requiring little pruning to maintain its neat habit, and like all Cephalotaxus it is left alone by deer. Site it in humus-rich, well-drained soil and keep it out of hot afternoon sun, which can bronze the foliage.
sources: JC Raulston Arboretum at NC State University

common_name: Hedgehog Plum Yew (Dwarf Spreading Japanese Plum Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, average garden soil in partial to full shade; this Iseli introduction can be sheared lightly to maintain a dense edging habit if a more formal line is wanted.

directions: An Iseli Nursery introduction, this dwarf spreading plum yew carries longer, deeper-green, glossier needles than other low-growing selections, giving the mounded plant a noticeably denser and more lustrous surface. Its slow, steady spread and tidy habit make it a durable substitute for boxwood as a low hedge or border edging in shaded sites where boxwood struggles with humidity and blight. Give it consistently drained soil and partial to full shade, and expect only a few inches of growth per year, which keeps maintenance minimal. As with the rest of the genus it resists deer browsing and tolerates the root competition common beneath established shade trees.

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; this species eventually grows into a small tree, so allow considerably more room than for the compact Japanese plum yew cultivars.

directions: A less commonly grown but botanically distinct plum yew from central and western China, this species matures into a large, loosely branched shrub or small tree with long, flattened, dark-green needles and the same non-toxic, plum-like fleshy fruit found on female plants of the genus. It tolerates the same deep shade and root competition that make Cephalotaxus valuable substitutes for true yews in humid climates, but its larger eventual size suits it better to woodland edges or naturalized plantings than to foundation use. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and expect slow, steady growth over many years rather than a quick screen. Like its relatives it is unpalatable to deer, making it a dependable choice where browsing pressure rules out other broadleaf or needled evergreens.

planting.note: Divide established mats or set out small rooted sections in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade; this golden form needs the same constant moisture as the green species and will crisp quickly if the surface dries out.

directions: This chartreuse-to-gold selection of Krauss's spikemoss forms the same dense, prostrate, scale-leaved mat as the species but glows with a warm yellow-green cast that brightens dim corners more than the plain green form. It spreads by creeping stems rooting at the nodes, gradually filling in as a living carpet over consistently damp shaded ground, terrarium substrates, or the base of container plantings. The color develops best in bright, indirect shade — deep, dark shade mutes the gold tone toward green, while any direct sun scorches the delicate foliage outright. Keep the soil evenly moist at all times, since this cultivar has no more drought tolerance than the species and will brown within days of drying out.

planting.note: Divide small clumps and set out in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in shade; unlike the flat-spreading species, this cultivar mounds upward and works especially well tucked between stones or in shallow containers.

directions: Rather than creeping flat across the ground like the species, this dwarf selection piles its tiny whorled leaves into tight, rounded cushions only a couple of inches tall, giving it a moss-like bun shape distinct from any other spikemoss form in cultivation. The dense mounding habit makes it a natural fit for fairy gardens, trough plantings, rock crevices, and terrarium foregrounds where a miniature, sculptural texture is wanted rather than a spreading mat. It shares the species' demand for constant moisture and high humidity, browning rapidly if the growing medium is allowed to dry, and performs best tucked into shaded, sheltered spots protected from drying wind. Divide congested cushions in spring to propagate new clumps or to keep the mound from becoming overly dense at the center.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this East Asian spikemoss is grown outdoors mainly in warm, frost-free climates and elsewhere is best treated as a terrarium or container specimen.

directions: Native to shaded rock outcrops and forest understory from China south through Southeast Asia, this spikemoss produces slender, arching, repeatedly branched stems clothed in tiny bright-green scale leaves that give the whole clump a soft, ferny appearance quite different from the flat mats formed by many of its relatives. It slowly builds into a loose, spreading clump rather than a tight groundcover, making it more useful as a textural filler among shade perennials or in a hanging basket than as a solid carpet. Consistent moisture and shelter from direct sun are essential, since the fine foliage has little reserve against drying out. Where winters bring hard freezes, grow it in a container that can be moved under cover, or keep it as a humidity-loving houseplant or terrarium subject.
